For *1917*, I think the obvious thing that fits your taste is the **cinematography and the illusion that you're following them in one continuous shot**. But I would not make it purely technical because the friendship and urgency of the mission are what give that filmmaking weight. 1917 is one of those films where the way it was made is almost as impressive as the story itself. The decision to make the film appear as one continuous shot is incredible. Rather than watching the war from a distance, the camera follows Blake and Schofield through everything. Across trenches, through fields, into abandoned buildings and eventually straight into battle. There’s rarely an opportunity to escape from what they’re experiencing, and that makes the whole mission feel much more intense. Roger Deakins’ cinematography is absolutely stunning. There are so many shots where I find myself thinking about how they actually managed to capture them, especially knowing how precisely the actors, camera crew, sets and effects had to work together to maintain the illusion of one continuous journey. The nighttime sequence through Écoust with the flares lighting the ruins is probably one of the best-looking sequences in the entire film. What really makes it work though is that all of that technical brilliance actually serves the story. The mission itself is incredibly simple: cross enemy territory and deliver a message that could save 1,600 men. Because you stay with Blake and Schofield for almost every step, you start feeling the distance, exhaustion and constant danger alongside them. The friendship between them gives it the emotional weight it needs too. What begins as two soldiers carrying out an order gradually becomes something much more personal, and there are moments that hit incredibly hard without the film needing to overdo them. I also love how the war is portrayed. It isn’t constantly trying to give you huge battles. Some of the most tense moments come from silence, empty trenches or simply not knowing what might be around the next corner. Then when the film does open up into something bigger, it feels enormous. And that final run across the battlefield while everyone else charges in the opposite direction is one of those scenes I could watch again and again. Brilliant cinematography, incredible attention to detail and a simple story made unbelievably intense by how it was filmed. Definitely one that made me appreciate just how much work can go into getting a shot exactly right.

Having watched Birdman before, the simulated continual shot was a style of interest to me and 1917 definitely delivered with its two shot style. Not only does 1917 pull this off smoothly, but with great narrative effect. What 1917 has to offer is a visual production and cinematography behemoth, earning its Oscars' multiple times over. This should come as no surprise from director Sean Mendes, whose work on Spectre (2015) and Skyfall (2012) share the larger-than-life visual style of Mendes, with Spectre including a long duration tracking shot commonplace in 1917. 1917 shows no qualms with the brutality on display that defined WWI and tells no lies in the unceremonious slaughter of millions. The reality of the matter is the trenches and the space between them were simply hell on earth. 1917 leverages its transition to the second continual shot to further drive home this hellscape. Likely in homage to The Iliad and Greek mythology at large, we cross the river and are shot in head and black out. We awake to a world in ruin, a dark, destroyed landscape lit only by towering fire and flash of guns. What I believe Mendes shows here is in tribute to the crossing of the River Styx into the land of the dead, and we stay in this hellscape until we cross the river once more to return to the land of the living. Cinematically, the time spent inbetween river crossings is some of the most visually stunning, emotionally evocative pieces that I have ever seen. That experience alone is worth seeing this film. While there are many things to praise about this film, to avoid being long-winded I'll keep it to this. 1917 is more than deserving of its accolades and is a flexing of Mendes' cinematic vision that pays off in a big way. Undoubtably worth your time. 8.5/10

Watched this with Eli tonight at Riverview, and it was the first time that I have seen it in a few years. I used to consider this my favorite movie and it was really really good on the rewatch. I think this time around I gained more appreciation for the reality that so much of the film was caught in the continuous shot, and it puts into perspective just how good the cinematography was throughout. The details of the scenes and locations were so intense and I felt like I was dropped into battle with them. I think the plot was better than I remembered too, and seeing the main character transition struggle from the opening part of the journey to carrying on Blake’s legacy was really special. I really enjoyed this film!

Breathtaking, stunning, immersive cinematic masterpiece that showcases the horrors of World War I into a ticking clock survival thriller. Director Sam Mendes successfully strips away the typical political grandiosity of historical war epics to focus on a intimate, terrifyingly immediate human story of loyalty and perseverance. The film’s best element is that it is crafted to appear as one continuous, unbroken tracking shot unfolding in real time. Legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins uses clever camera movements, hidden cuts, and brilliant staging to pull the audience into the trenches alongside the soldiers. It removes the detachment of traditional editing, making you feel less like a viewer and more like a third runner on the mission. Early in the film, Blake points out chopped down cherry trees, noting that the scattered seeds will still grow back. Later, when Schofield is floating down a river choked with dead bodies, white cherry blossoms gently fall from the sky. It symbolizes that life and beauty will eventually outlast the cruelty of war. The ending beautifully captures that while the physical war continues unabated, Schofield has undergone a profound internal shift. Through Blake’s sacrifice, he moves from being a numb, detached survivor to a man who fully understands the value of human dignity and emotional connection. George MacKay and Dean Charles Chapman carries the film entirely on their shoulders. As the camera rarely leaves them, their performances required immense physical and emotional endurance. Both delivered a remarkably grounded and physical performance. With a script that intentionally lacks heavy dialogue or prolonged exposition dumps, MacKay and Chapman had to communicate raw vulnerability, fear, and sheer adrenaline through their facial expressions and body language. MacKay in particular, received significant praise for carrying the emotional weight of the film's second half. His ability to portray a quiet, desperate resilience that keeps the audience invested in the human drama amidst the chaotic spectacle of war. Overall 1917 is a breathtaking achievement that demands the biggest screen possible. Even if the narrative path is straightforward, the sheer scale of craftsmanship makes it an unforgettable, heart pounding journey.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Que absurdo. Que experiência. Esse filme é brilhante. Entrei esperando apenas um filme de guerra bem avaliado pela crítica e encontrei uma produção que é uma verdadeira aula de cinema. Roger Deakins fez arte aqui. Isso é arte. Cada cena é espetacular e grandiosa, mas não apenas por capricho: o filme é eufórico e imersivo, fazendo você se sentir dentro da Primeira Guerra Mundial e presenciar de perto a falta de escrúpulos daquele cenário. A emulação de um plano-sequência durante praticamente todo o filme me pegou muito. A maneira como câmera, fotografia, atuação, cenografia, montagem e efeitos trabalham juntos para sustentar essa experiência é simplesmente impressionante. Narrativamente, a história é relativamente simples, mas isso pouco importa. O caminho é a história. A missão é apenas o ponto de partida para uma experiência cinematográfica extraordinária. Eu estou impressionado. Que filme.
